headings.title: Purge runtime data while preserving setup

html:
Configuration and storage

Inspecting Runtime

Administrators can open Runtime from the product menu, Chat menu, or Directory. The Installation scope shows effective configuration, startup inputs, engine limits, Gateway settings, inference profiles and the sources of those values. Saved changes that require a restart appear separately from the running configuration.

Choose Task to inspect a retained task and select an earlier run when available. Missing historical values show Not recorded. Current installation values appear beside captured values when they differ; changing Settings does not rewrite history.

Search includes collapsed sections and full expandable details. Load more shows the next 100 matches. Refresh retries observations; unavailable services leave last-successful values visibly stale. Export JSON includes the complete selected scope, regardless of the current search. Credentials are removed from the page, search and export. This surface never starts inference, executes tools or changes settings. Use an entry's editor link to change its configuration.

Saving Settings changes

Most ordinary controls on /settings save automatically shortly after an edit. Wait for Saved shared settings before leaving the page. Appearance changes can preview immediately, before their save succeeds. If autosave fails, correct any marked input or restore the connection, then use Retry save. A failed batch can have saved some of its settings already; retrying sends its pending values again.

An invalid auto-purge duration holds back that purge group's switch, duration and unit, while unrelated valid settings can save. Turning the purge switch off restores its last valid duration if needed, so an invalid draft does not prevent disabling deletion. Execution log capacity accepts a positive whole number of bytes written as decimal digits, including values too large for an ordinary browser number; exponent notation and fractions are rejected.

Background updates bring in shared changes without rebuilding the page and wait while general Settings edits are pending. Refresh explicitly reloads the form and can replace displayed drafts; finish or retry saves first. If only some values could be loaded, the page displays a warning and uses available defaults for missing data. Reconnect and refresh before relying on those displayed values.

Feature panels can have their own save controls. In particular, model endpoint and generation edits require Save Main or Save Helper in Model routing. Their role revisions and errors are independent of ordinary Settings autosave. Data export waits for pending general Settings saves and asks you to retry if they have not finished.

Saved startup overrides

Startup configuration has a separate revisioned save path. Its response distinguishes the running process's active values from effective values for the saved configuration, and reports whether a restart is required. Saving these overrides does not restart listeners or apply them to running services. Read the current revision before updating; after a revision conflict, reread and review the latest values before retrying. Reset removes overrides and reveals the retained bootstrap defaults, which may include imported configuration.

Managed secret fields use references to available environment variables. The saved file retains the reference; public effective/active views show whether the secret is configured. Storage-path changes use their own relocation checks and recovery lifecycle. See settings persistence and startup overrides for ownership, preview behavior, atomic saves and restart boundaries.

Saving and storage cleanup

Deletion disappears from history once the server has durably accepted it. Conversation/task payload collection becomes eligible after two seconds without task execution. Its background worker uses up to 30-second maintenance windows, starting at most once every 15 minutes; reaching two idle seconds does not promise immediate removal. New execution pauses cleanup, and large deletions take turns with smaller ones. Saving can finish while cleanup remains queued. The shared indicator distinguishes queued, paused, cleaning, waiting for save, purging, retrying, and complete states. See the deletion queue lifecycle for recovery and retained-evidence details.

Saving persists prepared cleanup under the current retention rules. When tasks are executing, the server saves without waiting for cleanup. A manual save also requests a maintenance pass for expired artifacts and old unregistered files; the save can finish while cleanup remains pending.

The server verifies the saved state before removing obsolete recovery copies and managed files. Shared artifacts and evidence needed by unresolved work remain protected. The yellow activity dot flashes while background maintenance is doing work; pending cleanup alone does not make it flash.

Graceful shutdown drains local work, prepares eligible cleanup, saves, and finishes file removal. It does not wait for unresolved remote jobs to finish. If cleanup fails after saving, the server reports Data saved; cleanup pending, retains the retry information, and exits. Cleanup resumes after restart. An unconfirmed save continues to produce a separate warning.

Startup restores deletion protection before accepting work and resumes physical cleanup afterward. Verified unchanged records are reused by the first save; real startup repairs are still saved. Older recovery formats remain readable. Their cleanup indexes are built during idle maintenance, so the first storage migration can take longer than subsequent deletions.

Auto-purge inactive conversations

Open Settings → Auto-purge → Conversation auto-purge to automatically delete old conversations. This shared setting is Off by default. Delete after inactivity has a number input and an Hours / Days selector. It defaults to 1 day (24 hours) and accepts positive whole numbers, with a minimum of 1 hour when Hours is selected. You can set the duration before turning Auto-purge on; the switch, number, and unit save together across browser sessions. Existing day-based settings keep their duration.

New prompts, tasks, epochs, and substantive execution progress or completion reset the timer for their conversation. Opening, viewing, searching, renaming, and background heartbeats do not. Pinned conversations and conversations with queued, running, paused, waiting, scheduled, monitored, or unresolved work are protected. Unpinning uses the existing activity time rather than starting a new timer.

Each conversation saves its enabled state and inactivity duration when it is created. Changing the duration or unit sets the default for new conversations; existing conversations keep their saved policy. Conversations created while the switch is off remain exempt from conversation auto-purge when it is enabled later.

Turning the switch off pauses new conversation deletion decisions. Turning it back on resumes previously enrolled conversations with their original policy and clocks; time spent off still counts. Already accepted deletions finish. The server checks on startup and every minute, even when no browser is open. Deletion is permanent; stored data is removed through the background cleanup queue described above.

On upgrade, older conversations and tasks that lack saved policies adopt the restored current settings once, preserving their activity and completion times. Already-expired records can remain due. Saved policies survive restart and backup restore; later default changes do not rewrite them.

Auto-purge finished tasks

Settings → Auto-purge → Task auto-purge is a separate switch, also Off by default. Delete tasks after finishing and Task retention unit default to one day; choose a positive whole number of Hours or Days. Each task saves its policy when it is created, before it starts or finishes. New tasks use the current default even inside an existing conversation. Older tasks keep their saved duration. Tasks created while the switch is off remain exempt from individual task auto-purge.

The countdown starts from recorded completion of a completed, failed or cancelled task. Accepted resume clears that clock; finishing the new work cycle starts a full countdown using the same saved duration. Viewing or renaming does not reset it. Pinned conversations are protected. Unpinning gives enrolled finished tasks a fresh countdown using their saved duration, even if task auto-purge was disabled at that moment. This differs from conversation expiry, which keeps the conversation's existing inactivity time.

Tasks needed by unfinished dependents, active attempts, pending input, queued follow-ups or unresolved execution remain protected. Unknown completion times also stay protected. A displayed deadline is an eligibility time; the server must recheck current work and ownership before accepting deletion.

Task labels use the last server observation and refresh while visible. A deadline reaching zero does not itself remove a row or send a deletion request. The task deletion and feedback flows explain how visible tasks request deadline observations and how accepted removal is separated from cleanup.

Task expiry removes that task's history and queues its owned payload cleanup, while keeping the conversation and its other tasks. Automatic task cleanup does not refresh conversation inactivity. Automatic conversation deletion waits until both its inactivity deadline and its enrolled tasks' retention periods have passed. This task retention hold also applies while individual task purging is paused. The conversation countdown displays this effective deadline. Finished tasks exempt from individual task auto-purge impose no extra hold: their conversation can still expire under its own saved policy. Unfinished or unresolved work stays protected.

Turning task auto-purge off pauses individual task deletion decisions without resetting saved clocks. Re-enabling resumes enrolled tasks; already accepted deletion intents continue through cleanup. Manual deletion keeps its existing review and protection rules.

Execution logs remain available after ordinary task completion. Accepted deletion or expiry can retire owned log copies, while shared receipts and unresolved Gateway cleanup retain the evidence still needed. See retention clocks and output retirement for the ownership and recovery rules.

Removable destination protection

Settings → Removable destination protection → Protect removable destinations is On by default for new installations. Existing saved choices are preserved. The preference is shared across tasks and browsers and persists after restart.

When enabled, recognized file writes and copy destinations are checked against the selected USB or external drive. A source path such as “everything in /mnt/models” does not select a destination. An explicit destination instruction, accepted destination parameter, or confirmed drive choice can select one; multiple eligible drives require a choice.

Directory inspection and dry-run copies do not require destination selection. Arbitrary scripts and unsupported command syntax continue through ordinary execution permissions; this optional check is not a filesystem sandbox. Disabling it bypasses destination checks for subsequent operations. It does not replay blocked commands, stop jobs, or change permissions or Resource locking settings.

Appearance

Settings → UI Preferences → Debug mode by default is off initially, including fresh installations. Off uses the compact, immersive conversation view; on shows the full detailed view. Use a conversation's Debug mode switch to override that default for the chat. Saved view choices are preserved when upgrading, and later changes to the default preserve each conversation's explicit choice. The default is shared across devices, while conversation choices are saved in the current browser and shared by its desktop and mobile interfaces.

Older saved Immersive on choices retain the compact view (Debug mode off). Legacy version-one Immersive off values follow the shared default, because those versions also saved off automatically without a user choice.

Open Settings → UI Preferences to change Font, Font size, or High contrast. Desktop chat also has More options → Appearance; on mobile, open Agent options → Appearance.

Opening the font picker automatically detects fonts available in your browser and adds them to the dropdown. Detection checks a shared catalogue of macOS, Windows, Linux, and common custom family names against text rendered on your device; it does not list fonts from the smTO server. This works when accessing a remote server and when the browser's font enumeration API is unavailable.

In browsers with Local Font Access, Load system fonts requests the full list your browser exposes. This requires HTTPS or localhost and browser permission; an existing grant loads the list automatically. Other browsers can only detect known family names they can render. Browser privacy restrictions can hide fonts, so automatic detection is not an exhaustive inventory. Safari in particular restricts user-installed font access.

For another family, expand Use another font, enter the Font family name, and choose Use font. Only the selected family is saved to the server. Detected lists stay in the current page, and font files are not uploaded. System default restores the device's default UI font. A selected font uses a fallback on devices where it is unavailable; code keeps its monospace font.

Use A− and A+ to adjust all app text from 80% to 200% in 10% steps. Reset to 100% restores the default text size without changing contrast. High contrast strengthens text, borders, and keyboard focus in either Light or Dark, and remains enabled when the theme changes. Defaults are 100% and normal contrast. Existing theme selection and browser zoom continue to work.

Font, font size, and high contrast apply immediately and save across devices connected to this application instance. If saving fails, the current page keeps the preview; choose Retry (or Retry save in Settings) to save it. These preferences cover the Agent UI and its management pages, including the dedicated mobile client. The standalone Manual and diagnostic sidecar do not consume this shared server preference stream. Their day/night choice and active palette can follow the browser's same-host cookies. Separate public sites keep their own appearance.

The theme editor adds per-theme color and font overrides and conversation backgrounds. Those settings belong to browser site data, not the server preference store. An active theme font overrides the inherited appearance font until cleared; server Settings export/import does not back up these local palettes, favorites or images.

Export / Import

After clicking Export JSON, a single status line shows the current export stage and estimated time remaining. The estimate adapts to measured progress; new exports may show Estimating…, and interrupted measurements show Re-estimating…. Stage changes use your activity-update animation preference. Leaving Settings while an export is running asks whether to stay or cancel; reloading or closing the tab uses the browser's standard warning. JSON ready · Download started means the complete backup has been handed to the browser's download manager. Backup flow diagrams trace browser and server ownership, cancellation, staged import and the startup commit boundary.

Open Settings → Export / Import to download a JSON backup or restore one from another app version. Export includes all 15 application stores: settings and runtime configuration, Parameter Store values (including secrets), conversations and messages, uploaded documents, generated artifacts, tasks, schedules, notifications, monitors, recipes, prompt templates, conversation notes, Memory, execution cache, traces and model-output history. The download contains plaintext credentials; store it securely.

Choose a JSON file to validate it and review the source version and record/file counts. Validation does not change existing data. Check the replacement acknowledgement and choose Import on next restart, then restart the app. Import replaces saved data; it does not merge conversations. Until restart, Cancel pending import cancels the replacement. Edits made after staging are replaced by the imported data. The current JSON size limit is 512 MiB.

The app rebuilds current database schemas before loading the records. Backup format and collection versions are separate from SQLite schema versions. Older records can omit newly added nullable/defaulted fields. Unknown versions, collections or fields, invalid settings, duplicate records, broken database references, invalid paths, and checksum mismatches reject the import before replacement. Changes that rename fields or alter their meaning require an explicit compatibility adapter; the importer never silently drops unfamiliar data or executes SQL from a backup.

Import applies before runtime stores and workers open. Temporary rollback material and a write-ahead journal restore the originals if replacement fails or the process stops midway. After verified replacement, the app removes that temporary material.

The running app uses RAM as its working state and retains one committed checkpoint on disk. Automatic saves run after the two-second idle grace; explicit Save and shutdown also flush changes. Saving builds one temporary replacement, verifies it, publishes it atomically, and removes the old save. There is no retained previous checkpoint or permanent extra repair generation. Native run state uses a binary snapshot with an independent mirror; other domains use SQLite and matching logical JSON recovery data. All representations belong to the same selected revision and rotate together. A verified native mirror can repair a damaged copy of that revision; it is not a backup of an older state. See Controller persistence for format, integrity and migration details.

Deletion is accepted durably before it disappears from history. The idle cleanup queue removes disposable records from RAM in bounded, rotating batches. The save worker serializes affected RAM domains into fresh native snapshots or database and logical recovery files, then replaces the checkpoint. Unchanged domains reuse verified bytes. Deletion never opens a database itself. Cleanup completes only after the old save and other application-owned recovery copies are removed. Pending remote work retains its required evidence and does not prevent startup.

Restored schedules are paused and unfinished tasks/runs are interrupted. Running external jobs are retained as lost/unknown outcomes, without adopting source process leases. Review connections and work before resuming. Destination database paths, workspace root and listener address/port remain local. External workspace/Gateway files, environment files, browser-only preferences/drafts and device identity keys are outside this backup. A different computer may need fresh Gateway pairing and license acceptance. Imported bootstrap configuration is saved in the settings store; UI settings continue to override its runtime defaults.

If an old SQLite schema prevents startup, use the CLI from the app workspace:

aor backup-export backup.json
aor backup-import backup.json
aor backup-import backup.json --replace-existing

The first command reads stores without opening schema-enforcing store constructors and refuses to overwrite an existing output file. Import without --replace-existing only validates and previews. Both commands accept --config PATH. Restart the single controller process to apply a staged restore; do not run another controller against the same files during replacement.

For maintainers: data_transfer/stores.py owns the store inventory and the migrate_records compatibility boundary. Keep wire versions stable for additive database changes, and add explicit adapters and historical fixtures for semantic or renaming changes. test_data_transfer.py covers the full inventory, old-schema export, missing-column defaults, rejection without mutation, and interrupted restore. The browser tests exercise Settings at desktop/mobile widths and both themes.

Settings → Capabilities → Automatic Capability Selection is on by default. The same switch in composer Options changes the next prompt on desktop and mobile. Automatic mode selects relevant permitted Skills before the Agent runs; Manual mode exposes the complete permitted set using ordinary discovery. In the Capabilities editor, Auto means eligible, Always means included in each selection, and Never excludes the capability. These choices support prompt, conversation, and global scopes. Selection does not grant credentials or approval. The activity view shows the selection, changes after steering, unavailable Skills, and any fallback to the accepted permitted set. Queued and scheduled work keeps the configuration captured when accepted; changing the default affects future work.

Agent Introspection, Task Context, Task Scratchpad (KV), Memory and Shell are always selected in both Automatic and Manual. Their Skills and tools appear as Built in · Always enabled, with no selection toggles. KV holds temporary working data for the task and its follow-ups; each new task starts with a fresh scratchpad. Memory tools can read and store information across tasks without a shortcut. Automatic lookup, injection, guidance, checks and proactive learning are off by default; add @use_memory to enable them for that task and its continuations. Each new task requires its own opt-in for automatic support. An instruction not to remember information still takes precedence over proactive learning.

File read (file.read) is also included whenever permitted, even when Automatic selection omits the Files skill. Other Files tools still follow normal selection. The Agent prefers bounded native reads for known files and read_result for omitted output already captured by a previous call. Files/tool exclusions, workflow limits, Advisory mode and Gateway availability continue to apply. Existing saved selections remain unchanged until a new selection is accepted.

Selection does not bypass execution permissions, Shell executable exclusions, workflow restrictions or Gateway prerequisites. Advisory mode permits local Memory but does not execute Shell commands. After installing this change and restarting the server, submit a new request. New requests normalize saved built-in exclusions independently of the automatic Memory opt-in; Resume, Continue and Restart without new intent retain the already accepted selection. See tool discovery and durable Memory.

The active Python configuration is src/agent_runtime/api/config.py:Settings. Runtime updates accept the explicit fields in AgentRuntimeControlsPayload. Mission Control uses a curated registry with schema_version: 2; internal runtime fields do not automatically become settings. UI preferences are stored by api/settings_store.py.

Settings → Security → Gate sudo controls server-side sudo handling and is on by default. When enabled, the server checks sudo syntax and uses managed local or verified remote elevation. When disabled, sudo commands pass through unchanged, including sshpass, sudo options, pipelines, redirects and command sequences. The server bypasses its sudo-specific checks and automatic elevation. Use the command's normal password input, stdin or terminal interaction in this mode; the managed sudo_password and sudo_username fields are inactive. Ordinary command permissions and the target operating system's authentication still apply. Changes affect subsequent commands, including active and resumed tasks.

Settings → Model routing owns separate Main and Helper endpoint, model, context and generation settings. Each role has an explicit Save Main or Save Helper action and revision-checked persistence. These edits are separate from ordinary Settings autosave. The Model Configuration guide is the authoritative explanation of profiles, recommendations, provider parameters, routes and accepted-request snapshots. A configured context ceiling cannot create capacity on the model server.

Inference-enabled controllers can bind a ready managed instance in Inference → Overview. This uses the same model settings, with an instance reference and verified launch generation. Inference → Caching also reuses Settings' prompt-caching editor. Inference profiles, private secrets, jobs and logs live in inference/ beside the current-run database; model/runtime/build paths remain separately configurable. See Inference management.

Capability selection timeout (seconds) is in each role's Generation and context controls. Its current schema defaults to 30 seconds and accepts 30–1,800 seconds. Save the relevant role for new work; accepted tasks retain their captured configuration. See the model guide for role assignment and fallback behavior.

UI preferences use PUT /api/agent/settings/preferences; supported general execution controls use POST /api/agent/runtime-controls. Loading Settings does not write displayed defaults back to the server. Model-routing choices belong to the revisioned role configuration; browser-local theme overrides and draft/return navigation have separate storage. Prompt history remains backend-owned.

Settings → Agent behavior → Prompts opens the separate Prompt Editor. Save custom instruction text explicitly; it applies installation-wide at the next model request. Shipped defaults remain sealed in packaged prompts.db, while userprompts.db stores customizations. Restoring prompt text does not change the independent compact-guidance selection settings.

Settings → Advanced → Ramble guard is enabled by default. It appends convergence guidance at the end of agent instructions on every execution turn, after skill and Task Contract guidance. The agent is guided to settle reasonably verified decisions, avoid repeated reasoning and speculative alternatives, and proceed when requirements are satisfied. New evidence, failed verification or an unmet requirement can reopen a decision. Turn it off to omit this paragraph from new tasks.

The backend preference is ramble_guard_enabled (strict boolean). For example, PUT /api/agent/settings/preferences with {"settings":{"ramble_guard_enabled":false}} disables it. Prepared, queued and scheduled tasks capture their setting when accepted; resumed and restarted tasks keep that value. Older tasks use the enabled default.

Settings → Advanced → Context-efficient execution is enabled by default. It guides the agent to inspect scope, use bounded reads and batches, keep script output compact, and save large intermediate data to files or results for exact retrieval later. Turn it off to omit this guidance from new tasks. Both modes retain the same tool-result preview, verification, parallel execution and compaction behavior.

The backend preference is context_efficient_execution_enabled (strict boolean). For example, PUT /api/agent/settings/preferences with {"settings":{"context_efficient_execution_enabled":false}} disables it. Prepared, queued and scheduled tasks capture the setting when accepted; active, resumed and restarted tasks keep that value. New tasks in existing or forked conversations use the current setting. Checkpoints and prepared requests from before this setting existed use the enabled default.

Settings → Advanced → Automatic Python correction is enabled by default. It corrects supported Python entrypoint shapes before execution, with no model call. For python.run / python__run, source without main(inputs) can be treated as an intended function body and wrapped, including callbacks, helper defaults, nested definitions and ordinary control flow. This does not promise equivalence to running the original text as a module, or prove that it will succeed at runtime. The candidate must compile and pass the existing validator; bare main conflicts and a generated generator/coroutine entrypoint are rejected.

Transforms retain the conservative simple-script/plain-helper rules. Existing entrypoints also retain their narrower repairs: moving eligible imports/helpers inside and removing an exact redundant trailing call or guard. Correction invents neither returns nor calls to helper-only scripts, repairs neither syntax nor runtime errors, and does not bypass safety or permissions. Unsupported source follows the existing model-correction path. Turn it off to keep strict rejection of malformed entrypoints (python_entrypoint_required for python.run).

The backend key is python_entrypoint_auto_correction_enabled, a strict boolean in the existing preferences API. Prepared, queued, durable and scheduled tasks capture it when accepted; active, continued and restarted tasks retain their captured setting. Missing historical values default ON. This preference is independent of Agent Checks and generic tool-argument normalization.

The Agent UI model dropdown discovers all models from the configured LLM endpoint's /models API. Select a model to use it for new requests; the server saves the exact choice with this conversation. Use Refresh models after changing the served models. The list also reloads when returning to the window. A configured llm.default_model is preferred if the endpoint exposes it; otherwise discovery selects the first available model. New configurations default to auto. Saved unavailable models remain visible and block Send until you choose a replacement. Existing runs retain their original model when resumed.

Database settings are database_enabled, database_default_limit, database_max_rows and corresponding AOR_DATABASE_* environment variables. Retired SQL-agent aliases are unsupported; configuration uses these current names. The workspace option is workspace_cwd_guard_enabled and explicit monitor drafting is monitor_drafting_enabled.

Mode IDs are conversation, agent, advisory (standard is a historical read alias). Approval mode is manual or full_access. Retired settings are filtered at the input boundary and are not active configuration knobs. The generated environment and route references show active source consumers.

Conversation, task, event, monitor, and parameter stores remain isolated by their configured paths. The current-run database stores journals, receipts, artifact scope links and jobs. Preserve credentials and provider stores during upgrades; do not treat generated test state as user data.

Reusable HTTP target configuration belongs to Parameter Store, not the Settings preferences store. Create it with the HTTP Connection template and use @name in Chat. Credentials remain inside the same sensitive Parameter record; cookies, CSRF and OAuth session tokens remain volatile HTTP runtime state. Existing saved profiles need no datastore migration. See Parameters.

Composer preferences are durable per conversation: mode, gateway selection, model, behavior effort, summarization, Generate prose and Task Contract compilation/integrity. Desktop and mobile share them. Global preferences initialize new conversations and do not rewrite existing profiles. The four quick scheduling controls use existing conversation policy scopes; advanced This prompt overrides apply once. Secure Prompts is retired. Settings → Redaction provides 20 independent switches, all on for new installations; see policy lifetimes.

New Chat starts from current defaults. Settings changed before its first accepted task are kept in memory and materialize when the task is accepted; an unsent page reload resets them. Legacy conversations recover known choices from their latest accepted task. Missing or corrupt execution selections require an explicit replacement. Forks inherit allowed convenience choices, with fresh authority scopes; deleting a conversation removes its composer preferences.

Fresh-state baseline

This release requires explicitly supported, versioned state. An empty chat list does not establish compatibility. SQLite owners check their declared minimum and current schema versions; unversioned databases with application tables and schemas outside that range are rejected without replacement or deletion. Native binary recovery accepts only registered catalog identities and their explicit migrations. Recognized older formats can therefore remain readable; arbitrary older or newer state is not automatically upgraded.

Back up the complete old state directory. Start with a new empty directory using AOR_AGENT_STATE_DIR, and ensure any per-store path overrides also point to fresh files. Do not copy individual old databases into the new directory. Use a matching older runtime to access the backup. Current state created by this release supports normal restart, queue recovery and conversation continuation.

Fresh stores create their complete schema directly. The browser rebuilds tasks from the server queue and ignores retired local queue snapshots. Current settings, native journals, prepared policy snapshots, HTTP v3 profiles and Parameter Store Gmail authorization are written in their supported formats at creation. Missing accepted snapshots block execution; reads do not reconstruct them from old task history.

New installations seed portable product preferences: automatic day/night theme, Ubuntu font (with system fallback), Roll activity updates, hidden wavelet timeline, Task Skill context retrieval, 6,000-character head and tail tool previews, Ask permissions with Gate sudo on, and monitoring of disabled Agent Checks. All 31 Agent Checks, all 20 redaction sources, and removable destination protection start on. Unsafe actions require confirmation. Workspace CWD protection and tool resource locking also default on. Users can disable individual protections in Settings and scope Agent Check overrides to a conversation, prompt, or run.

Task concurrency defaults to two. Foreground, background and dependency activity limits are 16; resource scheduling uses custom limits with eight total/per-Gateway activities, 16 for heavy resource classes, eight lightweight/unknown and four observations. Model transport timeout is 1,800 seconds; the no-actionable-output timeout is 300 seconds. User edits persist across restarts, and accepted tasks keep their captured settings. Installation presets do not replace saved preferences; existing stores retain historical fallbacks for missing UI preferences. Missing Agent Check, workspace guard, and tool-locking settings use the enabled product defaults.

The preset contains no personal name, Gateway address, credential, workspace path or model tuning. The product name remains the default, context capacity stays on Auto, thinking budget stays at 50%, and generation parameters use provider defaults.

Server updates

Settings → Setup → Server resources controls the server process's open-file limit, including sockets and pipes. The default is 65,536. Administrators can use Save & Apply to change it immediately and persist it across server starts. The panel shows the configured value, effective limit, and OS hard maximum. Values must be whole numbers of at least 1,024 and cannot exceed the OS maximum. At startup, an OS maximum below the saved value caps the effective limit; the panel shows that the configured value is not active. Unsupported operating systems show an unavailable control. Newly launched child processes inherit the limit; existing child processes and remote Gateways retain their own limits. Settings are stored in server-resources/settings.json beside the installation's .auth directory and apply to all accounts on this server.

Settings → Setup → Server updates shows the installed compiled build, available release, progress, blockers, and last result. Its repository setting is independent of Gateways; leave it empty to disable discovery. Installation always requires an explicit action. Update from URL → Check package → Install selected build reviews an HTTPS package and its matching descriptor before accepting that exact build.

Accepted updates queue new tasks and wait for admitted work, including paused tasks and approval waits. Loaded managed models stop during final shutdown and retain their running intent. Access is briefly interrupted while the server restarts. Cancellation is available until shutdown starts. A failed final save retains the server process and offers Retry final save on the shutdown screen. Failed startup triggers an attempt to restore the compatible previous installation. Confirm the reported outcome: rolled_back means the previous build became ready; rollback_failed requires recovery and must not be treated as a successful restart.

The independent helper waits for a final-save receipt naming the accepted update before replacing the Server. It does not impose a shutdown kill deadline while controller RAM may still be authoritative. See the replacement boundary for the descriptor, helper and readiness owners.

The controller coordination flow explains which work may finish during draining, why new execution waits, and how checkpoint confirmation differs from the final-save receipt. The operator guide includes package selection, startup timeout, diagnostic records and release qualification commands.

Updates preserve the platform and server variant. Source installations and legacy packages require a manual update; an existing compiled installation needs one manual installation of an updater-capable release before this control can install updates.

Monitor disabled Agent Checks

Settings → Agent Checks → Monitor disabled Agent Checks is stored as the strict boolean disabled_agent_check_monitoring_enabled in the existing Agent UI preferences namespace. Fresh installations seed it ON alongside the Agent Checks preset. Existing installations keep their saved settings; missing settings and legacy saved work still resolve OFF. Individual check switches and the Disable all action remain independent.

ON enables local assessment and informational Activity notes with Learn more for disabled checks. It adds no model calls, approval prompts or enforcement. The accepted task/run snapshot owns the value through queueing, resume, restart and continuation; changing Settings applies to future accepted work.

Tool result preview

Desktop Settings and mobile Advanced provide two numeric controls: Head characters and Tail characters. Both default to 6,000. Values must be nonnegative integers with a positive combined allowance; either side may be zero. The global setting is tool_result_preview: {head_characters: 6000, tail_characters: 6000}.

Changes apply at the next model-input preparation, including running, queued, scheduled, resumed and restored tasks. Compact, Full and Adaptive delivery modes have been removed. Old settings links open the new controls; writes to removed settings return an error naming the replacement. Existing installations receive the defaults unless valid new values are already saved.

Task Skill settings are unchanged. See context and memory for preview, recovery and capacity behavior.

Purge runtime data while preserving setup

Open Settings → Storage → Preview purge. The preview lists the controller and all configured Gateways, estimated storage, active work, and unavailable targets. Sign in as the installation owner and type PURGE RUNTIME DATA exactly to start. Deletion is permanent. Active work stops, services restart, and progress survives browser reloads and process restarts.

The purge preserves settings, parameters, secrets, permissions, accounts, licenses, pairing, device identities, saved Memory, workflows and revisions, prompt templates, schedule definitions and saved monitors. Managed documents and artifact bodies referenced by retained definitions survive with their obsolete conversation links detached. Workspace files, repositories, build outputs, installed runtimes, model downloads, exported user backups and system logs are outside the purge.

All conversations, including pinned conversations, tasks, queues, runs, results, traces, model-output captures, execution caches, notifications, observations, job receipts and obsolete recovery generations are deleted. Unreferenced managed uploads, generated artifacts, scratch and transfer staging are removed as well. This bypasses normal retention eligibility. Enabled schedules and saved monitors resume in fresh contexts when their required Gateways are ready; missed schedule triggers are not replayed. New automation can create fresh runtime data immediately.

Unavailable Gateways remain pending; older versions without the maintenance capability require an upgrade. Pending targets cannot execute work. Reconnection retries their cleanup; Retry pending targets retries blocked targets after the cause is resolved. A successful preview is an estimate, not a guarantee that all preserved setup can be recovered. A target is never marked successful while process termination, storage ownership or retained setup is uncertain. Shared managed directories with another instance's ownership evidence remain blocked rather than deleting that instance's files.

Offline recovery

Stop the selected service and its automatic restart manager first. Use the same account, configuration, state-directory environment variables and instance selector as normal startup. Offline recovery acts only on the local installation; server recovery records Gateways for reconciliation after startup. Even dry-run requires exclusive local ownership. A successful local command can leave the overall operation partial until pending Gateways complete. Finish or cancel any pending storage relocation first, and keep the configured store paths unchanged while the purge journal is unfinished.

# Server source installation, from the repository root:
./startup.sh runtime-purge --dry-run
./startup.sh runtime-purge --confirm "PURGE RUNTIME DATA"
# Add --config /path/to/app-config.yaml when using an explicit configuration.

# Linux Gateway source installation:
./src/gateway_agent/startup.sh runtime-purge --instance example --dry-run
./src/gateway_agent/startup.sh runtime-purge --instance example --confirm "PURGE RUNTIME DATA"
# macOS uses src/gateway_macos/startup.sh with the same arguments.

Windows supports src/gateway_windows/startup.ps1 runtime-purge -DryRun and src/gateway_windows/startup.ps1 runtime-purge -Confirm "PURGE RUNTIME DATA", with -Instance, -Port and -TlsStateDir selectors. Packaged Server and Gateway executables accept runtime-purge --dry-run and runtime-purge --confirm "PURGE RUNTIME DATA". Gateway recovery also accepts --tls-state-dir and --port. Restart the service after offline completion.

Recovery reads preserved collections independently of disposable history. If a preserved collection is corrupt or missing, recovery stops and names it; it does not substitute installation defaults. Current checkpoints include independently readable native setup and Gateway policy data for this purpose. A damaged replay cache is cleared only after holding exclusive authentication ownership for the full replay window; pairing keys remain intact. Disk-write failures leave a resumable journal. Free space or resolve the reported ownership problem, then run the same command again. Once deletion starts, recovery only moves forward.

The controller API uses /api/agent/runtime-purge/preview, /start, /status, /{operation_id} and /{operation_id}/retry. Start returns an operation ID with HTTP 202. Gateway maintenance is owner-authenticated over HTTPS or the paired outbound connection and is never exposed as a model tool. See the runtime-purge architecture for the save, restart, generation replacement and remote verification boundaries.

Settings → Agent behavior → Memories opens the Memory Editor for saved memory content, tags, and recall details. It uses the existing Memory store and checkpoint persistence.
